content.en: The **Money Multiplier** represents the ratio of the total money supply in an economy to the **monetary base** (or reserve money). In the Indian economy, when the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** injects liquidity, commercial banks do not keep all these funds as reserves. Instead, they lend a significant portion to borrowers. This process of lending and re-depositing creates new demand deposits, effectively multiplying the initial base money. The extent of this expansion is constrained by the **Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)** and the **Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)**, which act as leakages in the credit creation process.

content.en: Students often confuse the money multiplier with the fiscal multiplier; remember that the money multiplier relates to banking and liquidity, while the fiscal multiplier relates to government spending.
